html:
The French Revolution was the upheaval in France that began with the meeting of the Estates General in May 1789 and ended with Napoleon's seizure of power in November 1799. It overthrew the monarchy and the privileges of nobles and clergy, and its ideas of rights, citizenship and the nation shaped modern politics.

The crown was bankrupt, largely from wars, including help to the American revolution, and the nobles would not pay more tax. Bread prices were high after the bad harvest of 1788, a strain linked to the cold climate of the period. Writers of the Enlightenment such as Voltaire had taught a generation to question church and king.

Main stages:

  • 1789: the Third Estate declares itself a National Assembly. Crowds storm the Bastille on 14 July. Feudal privileges are abolished and the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen is issued.
  • 1791: a constitutional monarchy. The king tries to flee and is caught.
  • 1792: war with Austria and Prussia, the fall of the monarchy and a Republic.
  • 1793 to 1794: Louis XVI is executed. Under Robespierre and the Committee of Public Safety, the Terror sends thousands to the guillotine, and the army is rebuilt through mass conscription.
  • 1795 to 1799: the Directory, a weak and corrupt government, kept going by its generals.

The Revolution's wars carried it across Europe. Its legacy is mixed: equality before the law, the end of serfdom and church tithes, the metric system and votes for (some) men on one side; terror, civil war in the Vendée and military dictatorship on the other. Napoleon wrote its gains into his Civil Code. Ever since, left and right have been measured from where people sat in its assemblies.
